utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Tuesday, February 12, 2008. Let me greet the Prosecution, the witness, as well as Mr. Seselj and everyone assisting us in this trial. Today we're going to proceed with the examination-in-chief of the witness. Let me remind you that the Prosecution used one hour and 25 minutes. It was given four hours originally. Therefore, the Prosecution have two hours and 35 minutes left. Let me tell the Prosecution that if you produce video or a document, I would like you to tell us what is the date of the document, of the material, the origin, in order to avoid any time-consuming objections. So please give this information about the material, date, origin before you put questions to the witness about the -- this material. If we proceed that way, we'll avoid objections. It might not be possible, for example, if you have a document that does not have a date, but then you should tell us in advance. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must draw your attention to two problems. One of these problems I have been assisted with by the Prosecution, because yesterday I received a document which is part of my book, The Vampire's Ball. I disclosed this book in the set of 80 books of mine as early as 2003. It's a newspaper article talking about a rally before the Federal Assembly, and in fact it's the rally we spoke about on Thursday. And you remember that Mr. Mussemeyer did not know either where the meeting was held or on what date, but he did have all this information at his disposal, and this is evidence of that fact. I don't know if the Chamber has received the documents I received yesterday. He had all this information, but it did not suit him to present it, because he wanted this witness to say something different. You will recall that on Thursday when this witness was being examined a video clip was shown where the crowd is yelling, "Revenge, revenge." When asked by the Prosecutor what the revenge -- what revenge was being referred to, the witness said it was revenge because of the crimes committed by the Croats in World War II. However, if you read this text, you will see that the crowd was responding to the killing of Vukasin Soskocanin, the commander of the Borovo Selo defence, and it was thought at the time that he had been killed, whereas later on it transpired that he had drowned in the Danube. The Prosecution disclosed this to me yesterday, and I suppose to you too. The first page bears the ERN number 03474996. It's an article entitled "Masked ball before the Assembly," and it was published in the Belgrade daily Osmica on the 21st of May, 1991, and the author of the text is Zoran Krstic. I have to tell you this in order to draw your attention to the kind of methods being used by the Prosecution to -- to introduce lies into this trial. The second point I have to raise is this: Yesterday -- we saw an article in the journal Epoha last week, and we were told that the author was Dobrica Cosic. I immediately drew your attention to the fact that this was a falsehood, and then Mr. Mussemeyer said that it had been a mistake. Well, now look at this witness statement made in 2002. On page 9 of the addendum where this witness comments on certain exhibits. It says here that the article was written by Dobrica Cosic. It's 06030949, page 9. So it's not a mistake made by Mr. Mussemeyer at the last session. It is a trick plotted by the Prosecution as early as 2002. I'm drawing your attention to this because I feel that you as the Trial Chamber have to intervene in such situations and that the Prosecutor has to have certain sanctions imposed upon him. I insisted on this last time, and I insist on it now and it's up to you to decide how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj has raised two issues. Does the Prosecutor want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first reproach was that we -- I sent yesterday this article from Mr. Seselj's book, "A Masked Ball In Front of the Parliament." I did this because I was tasked by the Trial Chamber to give the date and the location of this video. We made a little research, as I may call this, and found this article which is exactly describing what happened at that day. Because it's ten pages long I didn't want to surprise the Trial Chamber and the accused with this and this is the reason I disclosed it already yesterday, to give everybody a chance to read it. And the other reproach Mr. Seselj made that I was using this video on purpose to -- to give a false impression to the word "Revenge." I remind the Trial Chamber that it was not the Prosecution who asked what the revenge was referring to, it was the Judge, as to my recollection. The second document where we say that the author was Mr. Coric, I corrected it last time. It was the impression in the Prosecution this article was always referred to as the Coric document, and this is because Mr. Coric is named on the first page of this newspaper and therefore we always refer to the Coric document which was wrong and I corrected it last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've taken note of your comments. Let me come back to the first issue though. Admittedly when you see a video where the crowd is calling "Revenge, revenge," if you put it in context, in the context of the indictment, then you can establish a nexus, a connection between the two, but if you put this video in the context of a crowd calling "Revenge," because crime has been committed in Borovo Selo against someone, then the meaning of the video is not quite the same. That's why it's so important when you produce a document to give us any type of relevant information, the source of the document, the place, the location it took place in, and so on and so forth. Therefore, we are in a better position to understand the document, because if the document is misinterpreted, then it could be given more importance or less importance than it should. That's the reason for the objections raised by the accused, but I believe that it will -- won't be any problem in the future. The Prosecution will be able to tell us, okay, this is from such-and-such person, from such-and-such date, and things will be much clearer. I've taken note of the comments of Mr. Seselj. I've taken note of your answer. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's another problem here. I know that it's not possible here in the courtroom to show entire -- the entire footage of the rallies I attended and the speeches I made. I know that fragments have to be presented here to have the most important parts shown, but I think that the Trial Chamber has to intervene every time that the footage is artificially produced. You were able to see for yourself how often that footage had been cut and how it was actually a compilation of different parts. This cannot be admitted. It has to be an entire fragment, and we who are viewing it have to be aware that it's an entire fragment. As soon as something is cut up, I know that it is useless. How do we know that something has not been inserted from some other footage? You will recall the BBC footage where some statements of mine are combined with other footage made somewhere else, who knows where. This again is a compilation that has no evidentiary value. It has no probative value. What is shown here on video has to be an entire piece of footage. As soon as we see that it's been edited and cut up and something might have been inserted, then it can no longer be admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. This is now on the transcript. This morning I was reviewing part of your testimony in the Milosevic case about that BBC programme, and you had challenged the entire thing. It's something I remember very well. And as a professional and well-informed Judge, I am supposed to take into account everything. And when viewing a video made -- that has been edited and with a commentary, then you have to put yourself questions, but the proceedings will help the Judges to draw conclusions based on footage that is not complete and that could have been intentionally or not manipulated. I'm now going to give the floor to the Prosecution for them to proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to refer to your last remark. We don't manipulate any video. If the accused has to object to something that it is not complete or other things are not correct, he may do this. We are in a position to play the whole video if it's necessary, just to show that nothing has been manipulated by the Prosecution. I will proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And refer to this video we discussed about. It was shown last time. I think it's not necessary to show it again. I only wanted to refer to the last sentence where it said -- Mr. Seselj would have said this: "The Croats can create their new state but only West of the Karlobag line. Everything east of that line is Serbian." Last time I had the possibility to put only one question. I want to ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, was this the typical way how Mr. Seselj spoke about the Karlobag line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When that line is in question, Karlobag, Ogulin, Karlovac, Virovitica, that is the typical way he spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like now to come to the state which Mr. Seselj had in mind, which should have been created as a Greater Serbia. Can you tell us what kind of relation to other ethnic compositions Mr. Seselj had in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what precisely he had in mind, but I do know that in that Greater Serbia that was advocated there was a concern that Serbs as a people should be protected. If they couldn't live in Yugoslavia, they would live in a Greater Serbia. But I never heard him speaking in positive terms of either Croats or Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how he spoke about Muslims and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke about Muslims that they were Serbs of the Muslim faith. I don't remember what he said about Albanians, but he said the same thing about the Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was he using derogatory terms in respect to these minorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if his comments about these minorities have been criticised in the media in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were, but I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who criticised this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was opposition papers and opposition politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if there have existed any restrictions for him to make these kind of remarks in the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to tell us how Mr. Seselj spoke about the Croats, the Croatian state and its leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said the Croats could have their state east of the border we have just mentioned. As for the leadership, he would call them Ustasha. He would say that about Mesic, Ante Markovic and the others. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to play another video. It's 65 ter number 6020. It's a video about the same event we spoke. It happened on the 15th of May in front of the parliament. The Prosecution does not know who is the originator of this video. The Prosecution got it on the 3rd December, 1994, from an unknown person. For the interpreters, it's V000-0101.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Vojislav Seselj: The power has not been constituted by democratic elections. It is a direct prolongation of Tito's despotism and tyranny. That power is especially represented by the second big sworn enemy of the Serbian people, Ante Markovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you confirm if this was a typical way how Mr. Seselj spoke about Croatian leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think that's how he spoke about them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can we have admitted this video clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P180.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to continue with another exhibit. It's the 65 ter number 411. This document has already been marked for identification under the number P39. It's an interview which Mr. Seselj gave to the German magazine Der Spiegel on 6th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you have a chance to read this article before you came or when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I saw this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, Mr. Seselj speaks in this interview about the amputation of Croatia and that he was the commander of the volunteers of Borovo Selo. What is the meaning of amputation of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the very word "amputation" means cutting off a part, a part of Croatia from the whole, probably for the purpose of achieving the Karlobag, Karlovac, Virovitica border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was this used also by other Serbian politicians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to come to paragraph 5 in the B/C/S version where it says -- the question is: "What borders would that be? The borders are meant from Greater Serbia?" And Mr. Seselj's answer was: "Aside from provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo, republics Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia and Montenegro should be attached to Serbia, as well as the territories in Croatia which are inhabited by Serbs with the border along the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line." Is this the area which Mr. Seselj meant to be Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: In the next article it is said by the journalist that that would mean that Croatia would be reduced to one-third of its territory, and

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ ANSWERED
utterances.text: "To as much as you can see from Zagreb cathedral tower. It is not enough to the Croats. We will take everything." Are you aware of this quote, and was this the way as Mr. Seselj referred to the reduction of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as he spoke about amputation, this would mean it would be reduced to the borders it had had. As for the displacement of 30.000 people from Rijeka, I don't remember that detail. I'm reading about it now. I do know that Zagreb cathedral was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can the volume be turned up? I can't hear the witness very well. I can hear the interpreters very well but not the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that Zagreb cathedral was mentioned and later on some politicians in Croatia quoted those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was the meaning that all what you can see from the tower of the Zagreb cathedral is only Croatia or was there a different meaning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means that Croatia would be so reduced that one would see its borders from the tower of Zagreb cathedral. That's a narrow part around Zagreb itself where the border with Bosnia is. As soon as you mention the view from Zagreb cathedral it would mean that the borders of Croatia would be greatly reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want you to comment on the part which is on page 2, paragraph 3, where it says: "And if Muslims oppose the attempt to be deprived as a nation status." And the answer was: "In that case they will be expelled from Bosnia." The question: "To where?" The answer: " To Anatolia." Do you know this quote from Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that quote, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Further down on page 2, second column, paragraph 8, Mr. Seselj said: "The question was you are the leader of your own volunteer army. What was -- what is your strategy? The answer: I am a duke. This title has been given to me by the oldest Chetnik leader alive, Momcilo Djujic, from California. I organise interventions by our guerrilla organisation, define aims of attack and points that have to be won." Do you know if this description from Mr. Seselj describes correctly his role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part, yes, that he was a duke and that he was granted this title by the oldest Chetnik leader alive, Momcilo Djujic, who lived in the USA, but I don't remember this other part about the guerrilla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Next question, it's on page 2, third column, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the Serbian version. "It is said 80 per cent of the Federal army are Serbs. Why don't you let them defend Serbs?" Mr. Seselj's answer was: "Because this army has not protected us Serbs till now. They only intervene when Serbs are fighting against Croats. When they appear, we immediately retreat. There are still some Communist commanders in it who have prejudice against Chetniks." Did Seselj's men act under the command of the JNA or did they act independently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't speak about all the places where Mr. Seselj's volunteers were, but as far as I know, up there in Western Slavonia there was no army in one area where Mr. Seselj's volunteers were. As for the other areas I wasn't there so I don't know if they were together or separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to come to another issue. This is the relationship between Mr. Seselj and Arkan. Do you know how their relationship was, and can you describe this to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, to the best of my recollection, and it was also in the newspapers and the press, there were some quarrels between Arkan, Mr. Arkan and Mr. Seselj. They were quarreling about who was the greater Serb and the greater patriot. So they would try to denigrate each other in a way. There was rivalry and mutual recrimination between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were they bragging about their deeds and to the deeds of their men on the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they each said that they were braver warriors than the other one, and better warriors and more honourable warriors than the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I with like to come now to the arrival of Mr. Seselj's volunteers in Croatia if there aren't any questions from the Bench. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have a question for the witness about the relationship between Arkan and Seselj. You stated that these two men were in conflictual relationship because each one of them said that he was a better patriot than the other but what I find relevant here is the following: I would like you to tell me if, according to you, there was an understanding between them, an agreement between them, or were there differences between them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's hard for me to answer that question, Your Honour. My feeling was that they were not in complete agreement, that they had two different approaches. Mr. Seselj was first and foremost a politician, and later on he joined in the defence of Serbian interests as he himself said, whereas Mr. Arkan, from the very first day, was a warrior involved in the war. So I think their approaches were different in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You answered my question. Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you tell us when the war broke out in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the war broke out, I would say, immediately after the Borovo events, which was towards the end of May when the incidents first started and they burgeoned and became a war conflict in June and July when the flames of conflict were burning. In 1991, of course. And later on in Western Slavonia, this was on the 19th of August, it started a little earlier in SAO Krajina, I don't know the exact date when it started there, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What happened on the 19th of August in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to mention first of all that just a few days before the 19th of August, which would make it the 14th of August, in Okucani the forces of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia stormed the place and they started by shooting around Okucani and there was a conflict between the local population and the police and it spread, the conflict spread. And then on the 19th of August, there was an all-out resistance or attack by the Serb Territorial Defence from Pakrac, Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, Orahovica, Podravska Slatina, Pozega and so on and there was a broader conflict between the Croatian police forces and the Serb Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So the openance of this war were the Croatian police forces and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning it was the Croatian police and then a few days later it was the National Guards Corps as a new army formed of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was the role of the TOs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it organised the resistance in all these municipalities and the Secretariat for National Defence established them of the municipalities that existed in Western Slavonia, the ones I've already mentioned. They carried out a mobilisation of the male population, and they had reserve uniforms that they kept in their homes. These people were armed, and they established some sort of military defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to show the Exhibit 65 ter number 584. Mr. Witness, do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already seen it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: For the others, for the Judges and the accused, this is a report on the organisation of the local Serb Territorial Defence, Western Slavonia, and it's from the 16th of October, 1991. Mr. Witness, did you ever saw this document and can you tell us if it is authentic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Judging by the names of the people on that list, or at least I know a part of those people, their posts, and, yes, the document is an authentic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can we please have admitted this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P181.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, there was a time -- or can you tell us if volunteer units arrived in Eastern and Western Slavonia and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as -- I don't know about Eastern Slavonia when they arrived. I heard that they were there. Now as regards Western Slavonia, I think that they started arriving sometime at the beginning of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who sent them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to what I'd heard they came from Serbia and they were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Only of the Serbian Radical Party or also from other organisations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, people said that they came -- that various volunteers came and movements, but on the ground people would rank them all together under the heading title of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did they call them volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party or in a different way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they referred to them as the volunteers or the Chetniks, depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have these volunteers been called by local inhabitants? Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the Territorial Defence Staffs asked for assistance in manpower so that they could -- so that the fighting would be easier in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you yourself see them arrive sometime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw buses on one occasion who were -- which were arriving towards Zvecevo late. It was already dark. Several buses arrived, and the people in them were dressed differently. They didn't just have one type of uniform. They had different badges and insignia on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: From which company were these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if these volunteers were already armed or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, they did have weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Weapons already when they left the bus? And what kind of weapons, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were military weapons, the PAPs. Semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they welcomed by the local population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people reacted differently. Some people were happy that somebody had come in to help them and not to be left alone. Other people were wary seeing who these people were. So it was wartime and people felt differently towards them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, you just said that it was war. The Prosecutor is going very quickly and there's some events that are not mentioned, so I'd like to go back a bit if I may. You said that in August, on August 14 -- on August 19 there was Pakrac, but on the 14th of August there were other incidents, and I thought I understood that the Croatian police entered in different towns, and at the time there was a conflict. Is this the way it was perceived on the field? Did you feel that the Croatian police was entering into towns, that at that moment the ethnical Serbians tried to get together within the Territorial Defence in order to oppose the arrival of the Croatian police? Is this what the source of the problem was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I started my answer, and I began with the 19th of August, but then I went back a few days before that event and which was the cause of all the events to follow. But in response to your question, I'd like to go back even further after what happened in Pakrac on the 2nd of March and the 1st of April in Plitvice and then the 1st of May in Borovo Selo, to those events. And later on what happened was that in the vicinity of Pakrac municipality, on Mount Papuk, the policemen wearing uniforms of the forestry workers wanted to enter into the depth of the Serb villages where the Serbs, at least the menfolk, had already started to take to the forests with weapons, and there was a clash between the Croatian police at the time and the Serbian Territorial Defence because they found themselves in the forest face-to-face, and this was a surprise, and there was fear amongst the Serbian population, this conduct on the part of the Croats, because there was a lot of talk about arming the Croatian police and Croatian guard, and then the Serbs self-organised. They created their own Territorial Defence in case the conflict spread. So, Your Honour, this was a play of nerves, who would yield first or who would move first. And that's what happened in Okucani. The Croatian police moved first. And let me add that it was -- this happened in Grubisno Polje too to the north of Pakrac. The other was to the south of Pakrac where there was also a clash between the Croatian police and the Serb population and then all the events, the fears, the waiting, resulted in a broader conflict, and so from all these places, from all these localities there were a settling of accounts, if I can use the term, to prevent any further incidents. Now, I don't know he what was in the head of the Territorial Defence commanders, what they wanted to achieve through these activities of theirs but I do know that a sort of all-out offensive, all-out uprising occurred in Western Slavonia and the 19th of August is marked as a day of uprising by the Croats. And the Serbs see that day as the day when they started defending themselves in an organised fashion from the further storming of Croatian police into a territory which was exclusively Serb apart from a few villages which were partially Croatian or where the Croats were the minority population in those generally Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you've just said which is very important to determine the origin of the problem. I sum up. So according to what you say, starting on March 2nd, 1st April, 1st May, 2nd Borovo Selo, then August 14, August 19, according to what you say, apparently the Croatian police came into villages that were mainly Serbian, and at the time it seemed that there was a resistance or even an uprising of the Serbian population who self-organised, procured weapons, and so on. Is this how things happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Second question: Why did the Croatian police, as of March 2nd, and then April 1st and so on, why did they engage into this kind of operation? What was their motivation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Croatia became a new state, was established as a new state, it changed its symbols. Instead of the star on the flag and on the caps and uniforms of the police and army, there was the chequer-board insignia which is the coat of arms of Croatia which the Serbs saw negatively during World War II, and the Croatian state wanted to establish a new police force in all the localities in Croatia. Where the Serbs were in the majority and where the Serbs had their police the Serbs put up a resistance in -- they resisted this new chequer-board insignia. And so the Serb police station separated because they did not want to come under the jurisdiction of the Croatian authorities, because they saw this new police force with the chequer-board as something they could no longer trust and have confidence in because the Croatian leadership said that there were too many Serbs in the police force, that there were too many of them in other places. That meant to the Serbs that new policemen should be brought in to replace the Serbs. So on the 2nd of March there was the conflict in Pakrac when the new Croatian police force wearing the chequer-board insignia came. I think there were some 40 of them who arrived in Pakrac and the Croatian police were disarmed because they were thought to be taking away the weapons from the police station. So the chief of the police station disarmed then and called in the reserve police force. And I would say that the Croatian state did this too quickly and the Serbs saw this as an imposition on them in these places without any psychological preparation before that. And so there was resistance and a conflict between the Serb police in those places and the new associated Croatian police who was given an assignment by the Croatian leaders to establish control over that whole area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understood what you said extremely well. So you were in Pakrac. You originate from Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor on the setting up of the Territorial Defence of Pakrac was headed by Zozo Vezmin [as interpreted]. There were three battalions, 13 companies, 1.740 soldiers: 1st Battalion, 540 soldiers; 2nd, 740 soldiers; 3rd Battalion, 450 soldiers. So these are very significant figures. Was this the reality on the field? Did the Pakrac TO really comprise more than 1.700 soldiers altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but they weren't soldiers of 19 or 20 years old. They were men from 18 to 60, ranging in ages from 18 to 60. So the figures are correct. And it was the Territorial Defence of military-able, active men who, according to their deployment, were in the Territorial Defence or the Secretariat for National Defence. They had their own records according to different branches and services. They had uniforms at home, all the reservists. All the reservists had their uniforms at home, but they were issued weapons subsequently, and I don't know how that was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm sure you will shed some light. There's one thing I don't really understand. At the time Croatia was a republic that had been first recognised by the Vatican, then by Germany, then by the international community. So it's a republic. Why is it that in Pakrac a TO is set up and a report is sent to the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian republic? Could you explain how this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that time when the report was compiled, Croatia was not an internationally recognised state. This is October 1991. I think Croatia was recognised on the 15th of January. I might be wrong there, but I'm not very good on dates, but I think that was it. 1992, which means several months later. Now, at that time Croatia was a component part of Yugoslavia still, and it was one national defence for the whole country, and each municipality had its Secretariat for National Defence with all the tasks and assignments for peacetime and wartime when it came to defence, and that is why the lists and records that we have seen here was compiled by the staffs at the Territorial Defence of the municipalities and probably the Joint Staff of Western Slavonia which was sent on - I don't know by what channels - up to the Ministry of the Republic of Serbia. So that was done by the TO staffs in 1991 when Croatia was still not a recognised state internationally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understood everything, in October 1991 when the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party arrived, the Pakrac TO depended and reported to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't claim whether it depended on it, but I know that the TO, for instance, relied on the Yugoslav People's Army, and through the Ban -- corps came to Okucani and reached the town of Pakrac itself. The Banja Luka Corps. And there was just one man - I think his name was Jovo Trbojevic - from the JNA he came from Novi Sad directly to Vocin, but the Yugoslav People's Army never went further than Pakrac municipality and the TO was linked to the JNA. Now, whether the JNA acted within the frameworks of the Ministry of the Defence of Serbia or something else I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. One last question and then I will give the floor to the Prosecution. When the Serbian volunteers arrived, when these volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party arrived in Pakrac, where were they housed? Were they housed by the TO or of their own accord? Did they decide where to find housing? Can you tell us how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the Pakrac region I don't think they were there. They went to Zvecevo, Vocin, Slatina, that area, more to the north where the Yugoslav People's Army was not located. All I can conclude is they went via the TO, because it was the TO which was in command at a local level in the municipalities. They were the local command. Now, I don't think they could set up on their own. They had to be led by someone, so I assume it was the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So what you say is the following: When they arrived in Pakrac, the TO sent them to Zvecevo, Vocin, Slatina. That's what you just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that the TO invited them to come in. Whether it was Slatina, Vocin, or somewhere else, that's how they came to come in and put up in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to continue with the volunteers. Mr. Witness, can you tell us what kind of reputation did they have among the local population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, different reputation. Some people liked them and relied upon them. Other people were afraid of them, depending on the experience that people had and the contacts people had with them, because Western Slavonia in World War II was a partisan area which -- well, there were Ustashas on the part of the Croatian army and the Partisans that were made up of Serbs and Croats. Serbs were in the majority. Now, the arrival of the Chetniks some people saw as -- that they should be wary of them, and -- because bad things were written about the Chetniks, whereas good things were written about the partisans. Now, some people relied on them because there was no other assistance coming in or other force that would help them in the war that was going on, and the Serbs had the feeling that they were left on their own. So the relationship towards them was different depending on people's experience of them. And because people were left to their own devices, people preferred to have someone with them, not to be left alone, to fend for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Seselj ever visited his volunteers in the area of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. That was sometime in late autumn. I think it was in October when Mr. Seselj arrived in Zvecevo and Slatina to tour his volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it also possible that it was in November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite possible. As I say, I don't remember dates that well, but it was late autumn, anyway. November, yes, November, because on the 15th of October, there was an exodus from Grubisno Polje and the defence of Western Slavonia was shaken by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Seselj on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet him. We were at a dinner together in Vocin with some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who accompanied him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly the people who accompanied him, but I think all together with him there were Veljko Vukic, Miljenko Miletic, I think Cedo Gacesa was also there and Petkovic, Veljko Vukelic, myself, and perhaps one or two other people. Not too many of us as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was there also a person called Ilija Sacic [sic], if I pronounce it correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Ilija Sasic. I think he was there too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Seselj on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We all talked amongst ourselves, discussed the general topics, the state of affairs in Slavonia and people who had taken part in the events spoke about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please shortly describe what was your relationship to Mr. Seselj at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't too close, but we did talk -- or, well, in the way people talk when they meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it correct when we say you had the same goals more or less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really think so. Not as far as political goals are concerned and as far as -- but as far as the war is concerned, well, no there, too, because I was exclusively in favour of a peaceful solution, whereas Mr. Seselj was a leader, and as such he accepted combat as a means of resolving the issue when it came to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: After the volunteers had arrived in the area of Western Slavonia have there been committed any crimes, do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, I think you're going too fast. There's a dinner that the witness is attending with Mr. Seselj. It might be good to know whether during that dinner there were any conflicts or any disputes among all these people or whether they shared the same objective. So there's this dinner in Vocin. During the dinner did you express openly your own solution, which seemed to be a more peaceful solution, and did Mr. Seselj mention the problem but calling for a military solution, or did you just talk about, you know, the weather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the dinner wasn't in Vocin, it was at Zvecevo, and at the dinner -- well, there was the general topic. We didn't discuss any concrete military action. My standpoint was well-known to most of the people who attended. I did not present my views because that was neither the place nor the time to do so, and my compatriots were in the Territorial Defence, so I was different from them, and we didn't discuss any military operations and conducting them in the defence of Western Slavonia, but the general situation what was happening in Serbia. People wanted to hear about things they didn't know about because they were cut off from the events there in the environment in which they lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you remember, what did Mr. Seselj say on that day? Do you remember? Yes or no? Because when you meet Mr. Seselj, I'm sure you remember that. So do you remember what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nothing special. He didn't say anything particular that I could recall now and tell you. They were just general topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did he talk about his own arrival and the arrival of the volunteers from his party? Did he expound on this? Did he say why he was doing this or was this just not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He just mentioned that he had come to tour his volunteers, to talk to them, to see how they were, what the problems were, how they felt, and then he toured his volunteers the next day, people from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he came was he wearing civilian clothes or military clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was wearing a military uniform, the camouflage uniform. It was the standard type of camouflage uniform that was worn at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time anyone could have a camouflage uniform without any problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite a lot of people had camouflage uniforms. I don't know how they came by them. At the beginning it was difficult, at the very beginning of the war, but later on the Yugoslav People's Army uniforms arrived and they were -- or, rather, that uniform was worn more than the JNA-type uniform. So people managed to come by these camouflage uniforms more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last detail. Was he seemingly wearing a weapon or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. At the time could one walk around carrying arms when one wasn't a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time there were few people walking around without weapons. Those were rare individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you yourself, did you possess a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not carry a weapon. And I was always in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: My question was: Do you know if crimes have been committed in Western Slavonia by the volunteers after their arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of 1991, we heard about crimes that happened in Western Slavonia. A number of them was ascribed to volunteers up there to the north of Vocin, and those around Pakrac were ascribed to Serbian extremists among the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the victims were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the victims were 90 per cent Croat, and a small number were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were they all -- people of all ages, or were they more or less older people? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were mostly elderly people if we're talking about Croats, because the younger ones had left the area and gone to Croatia proper. Whether they were joining the Croatian army or police, I don't know that, but I know that it was mainly elderly people who remained in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness a map which is 65 ter number 2868. It's map number 17 of the mapping binder. While we are waiting on the loading of the map, could you already tell us in which locations these crimes happened? Can you give us names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Balinci, Cetekovac, Vocin. I can't remember all of them. And some more places if we are talking about the northern part. Could we possibly enlarge this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We no longer hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try and speak up. The interpreters have difficulty hearing you. Please speak up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. To see better I have to come closer to the map. I'm short-sighted, and the glasses don't help all that much. Hum, Voceski - can you raise the map please - Vocin, Macute, Bokane, Ceralije, Balinci, Cetekovac. Yes, those are the places that are mentioned along with Sekulinci, Kraskovic. Those were the places that were mentioned as sites of crimes against non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if this map is depicting in the correct way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are discussing crimes. Which ones? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in those places elderly people who remained living there were killed or beaten up. Some people who were middle-aged as well, they were beaten up or killed by Serbian volunteers and the Serbian Territorial Defence. They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened in Vocin in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in December when the Territorial Defence and the populous withdrew from Slatina and Vocin and other places, I believe Croat civilians of middle or elderly age were arrested and beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have there been killings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were killed. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know when these killings happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime towards the end of December. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it possible that it was more to the middle of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. From the 10th until the 23rd December grave incidents took place. There was a large exodus of the people, and in several places there were killings, beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the disappearance of four young Croat men at the beginning of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who committed these crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I heard from other people. It was believed to have done by volunteers who did it together with the Territorial Defence of those places.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I believe that you have already realised that the Prosecution is leading this witness through hearsay. First of all, the witness doesn't even claim that he knows something reliably. He says it was being said. I believe the Trial Chamber should intervene every time you hear the words "it was being said" because it's hearsay and you can't even take it as indirect evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to say something before Mr. Seselj took the floor. These four Croatian men, the Prosecutor said that these men disappeared. What I felt was what did the Prosecution mean by this? The people were no longer there and went elsewhere, or were they killed and the bodies were found. So do you know anything? Don't you? What can you say about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, during those days, Your Honours, people disappeared on all sides. That happened too. I don't know for a fact whether they were found later dead or alive, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say the people disappeared, what do you mean by this when you say "disappeared"? Does this mean that on one day these people were in their houses and the next day they weren't any longer? So the people were perhaps no longer in their houses because they had left elsewhere or because they had been killed? So when you use the word "disappeared," what meaning do you attribute to this word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when you say someone disappeared, that means nobody knows where they were gone, what they were doing, whether they were alive. You know that there is a great number of people still on record as missing. It is suspected that most of them were killed, but nobody knows where their remains are. There are about 50.000 people still recorded as missing in Croatia. They disappeared in the winds of war. Nobody knew where they were. They couldn't just have left without telling anyone. They could have disappeared only in the sense that somebody took them away and killed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Croatians did someone tell you that these young people had been arrested and had disappeared after that, or is it that the rumour had it -- the rumour had it that these four young men had disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I only heard the rumours because I wasn't close to those localities and I had no direct contact with anyone involved. Those four were not a solitary incident. It was happening all over that area. I was not there, and I really had no direct insight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor showed you a map a while ago. A number of localities are circled in red. According to the Prosecution, that is allegedly where the crimes were committed. According to what you know, you were a local personality as far as these crimes are concerned. And these people who disappeared, were inquiries conducted during the events, after the events? Today what can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not a local resident there. I was 50 kilometres away from those places so I had no direct insight. I don't know whether the investigation was done then. I know the Croatian police investigated after the war. They did gain some information. I don't know how much. The only thing I heard during 1992 was that there occurred mistreatments and killings of Croats in those places. I didn't know the exact number. Later on in Croatian media, in the Croatian judicial system, inquiries and investigations were made as to what exactly had happened, who was killed in which way, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you had heard about this in 1992. Who told you and how did you get to know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that from Mr. Mladen Kulic who lived in that area during the war and spoke about these events and the victimisation, but he didn't provide any details. He spoke in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is -- who is Mladen Kulic? Who is this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's a man who lived in Podravska Slatina, and during the war he was part of the Territorial Defence and lived in the area of Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before we continue, I want to say for the Prosecution that we are well aware that this witness is only a hearsay witness. I think it came out from my questions, but hearsay is possible in this institution. And if everybody realised that this is a hearsay evidence, it is what I intended to show. Can I have please admitted the Exhibit number 2868, the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P182.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness the next exhibit, which has the 65 ter number 936.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is an open letter from Helsinki Watch to the Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and General Blagoje Adzic, acting minister of defence and chief of staff of the Yugoslav army, concerning human rights abused by the Serbian government and the Yugoslav Army, and it dates the 21st of January, 1992. Mr. Witness, do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen this document at the Office of the Prosecutor. I believe I was given it to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you aware of this report, that it has been sent to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, it's obvious that the witness had never seen this document until the Prosecution showed it to him in proofing, and it's pointless to discuss the document any further. Anyway, this is a document by a totally irrelevant political organisation of anti-Serbian nature which makes it doubly pointless to discuss. This witness doesn't know how the document came into being, nor had he seen it contemporaneously, and in this way the document cannot be introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is true that he does not know about the document given that the document had been addressed to Mr. Milosevic and to General Adzic, however, in the document itself there may be events which he is aware of. Therefore, the Prosecution can put questions to him relating to the contents of the document. Maybe he can confirm or deny things. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is exactly the reason I wanted to discuss this document with the witness. Mr. Witness, please have a look on page 5. For Your Honours it's page 4 in the English version, where crimes are described that should have happened in Cetekovac and Balinci. Mr. Witness, you already told us that you heard that these crimes had happened. Can you confirm if these crimes have happened in the areas mentioned here on page 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report speaks about the crimes in the localities I mentioned a moment ago. I see the details here such as the number of people said to be killed and victimised in these places. The places are right. I remember that well. Cetekovac, Balinci -- I really didn't know before the exact number of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who informed you about these crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people talked towards the end of 1991, and as for Cetekovac I heard of it earlier during the war itself. It was said that -- at least in the military circles it was said that there was fighting there. Later on it turned out civilians had been killed. Then I heard, during 1992, more about these events in Vocin. And when I say Vocin, that includes the area of Vocin including all the hamlets and villages around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecution has just indicated to you items that occurred on the 3rd and 4th of September in Cetekovac and Balinci. In three of these localities people were killed. I realise that this document talks about the Serbian forces without indicating which ones more specifically. On the second paragraph an event is being described which occurred in Cetekovac and the paramilitaries are mentioned, the Serbian paramilitaries. All of this is not very precise. What can you tell us about this, Cojlug, name of the third locality. Who would be the Serbian forces and who would be the paramilitaries according to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember personally and what was said and was happening there in Cetekovac, in Balinci, it seems that the members of the Territorial Defence of Cetekovac, Balinci and Vocin did it; it was ascribed to them. But when they say irregular Serbian army, they probably mean the Territorial Defence because it was the only force that existed then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll withdraw this objection immediately if you think it's inappropriate but it's obvious that these crimes happened a month before the arrival of the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. Therefore it's out of place for the Prosecutor to examine on that. It's irrelevant. You only warn me when something is irrelevant. You have never done so far with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I note everything that's being said and also what you say. This is the reason why I shall put a question to the witness. Those events which are being described are events which happened one month prior to the arrival of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you whether it's a month more or less, but at that time there were no volunteers in Vocin area or in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If the events, the crimes occurred in September and the volunteers arrived in October, you cannot accuse the volunteers of these crimes without being well-versed in inference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is a question to me, it is certain that at that time there were no volunteers, so you can't ascribe this act to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing to hide that at that time when these crimes happened the volunteers were not there. It's our intention to show what really happened, but may I please remind you that there is in the indictment against the accused there's also the JCE indicted and there is a certain relevance but it's up to you to make this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I wanted to go to page 10 for the Judges. It's page 9 of the English version. Here is described what happened in Vocin. Can you please have a look at it. Here it's mentioned in the second paragraph which deals with the events in Hum and Vocin that the White Eagles were responsible for these crimes. Who were the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What page, Prosecutor, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It's in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: In the English version -- oh, sorry. In the English version it's on page 9. It starts with December 19, "Hum and Vocin (municipality of Podravska Slatina)."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: My question was -- referred to the White Eagles. Do you know who were the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also volunteers who had arrived there to that area, and they also came under the heading of Serbian Radical Party volunteers, but I don't know whether they were really sent by the Serbian Radical Party or some other political organisation or movement within Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said they came under the heading of Serbian Radical Party volunteers. Who are you talking about when you said "they came under"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The local population saw all the volunteers as members of one group, representatives of a single political option, probably because Mr. Seselj was the only politician who came to visit from Serbia. So they were all lumped together as members of the same group. I'm not sure whether they were all from the same party, same group, or they came from different groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were also Mr. Seselj's men referred to as White Eagles when people spoke about White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the local populous lumped them all together and called them volunteers. They were one group, and the other group was the Territorial Defence. Since a lot of volunteers were from the Serbian Radical Party, they thought of them all as Serbian Radical Party volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now time to have a break. It is 10.00. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume. I will give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before I continue, I would like to have admitted the last exhibits we were discussing about into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P183.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to the admittance of this document because it has no relevance to the indictment. You have seen what the introductory part is like. It seethes with hatred against me and the Serb Radical Party and later on there is no information on any crimes committed by volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. On page 11, only one witness says that Chetniks, members of the paramilitary group led by Vojislav Seselj would arrive in small trucks with body bags. There may have been a truck with body bags indeed, but those body bags for Serb corpses, civilians, or soldiers who had been killed. Fallen soldiers if they were volunteers were transported to Serbia. Where is any relevance to be found here for volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party? I repeat that this is a political document. Certain facts are put forward. I might even agree with the facts, but the initial description saying that the most brutal group was the one led by Vojislav Seselj, the leader of the Serb Radical Party and the Serb Chetnik Movement, this is a purely political qualification and has no basis in the data presented later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges took note of your objection and we will see whether we need to overturn a decision regarding P183 after what you've just said. Please proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to have shown on the monitor the Exhibit number 6041, which is a video. Before the video is played I can give you the information that we received this tape from the Croatian government in 2001. It was recorded by the TV Benkovac, and the event happened on the 23rd of November, 1991. For the interpreters it's V000-3248.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "VS: That is not a Communist army and don't talk like that. "US: For me it still it is. "VS: Well, for you, for you. "US: That army betrayed me five times in the past three months in the battlefield. "VS: It betrayed you because of incapable officers in the field. Well, it's not like if someone is incapable - he is a Communist. Nonsense. It is one thing to be incapable, and a completely different to be a Communist. "US: Well we are in the army now. "US: Come on people, don't do this. "VS: We, the Chetniks, are also a part of that army today, and in Vukovar we also achieved ... Army officers command our Chetniks. We painted over almost all the helmets. Wait a second! On those army helmets we ... You know what, guys, I'm used to everybody being silent while I'm talking. Perhaps you still haven't developed this habit but I have. We painted two-headed Serbian white eagles on the helmets, and the army officer, captain, major, commands our people. And by coordinated action, also known as Kameni, our chief commander in Vukovar plans the action in cooperation with the Army Major in the evening, and they carry it out the following day. Because of soldiers deserting from their units, the army did not have enough manpower to go from house to house and take it over, so our people did that. Army strikes with tanks, mortars, Howitzers, and our people go from house to house and conquer it. And don't you tell me now that is a Communist army. They took off the five-pointed star insignias and did not ask us ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This video has already been admitted as Exhibit number P60, but we played a shorter version of it. What I was referring with this video is that Mr. Seselj said: "We painted White Eagles on our helmets." And I also wanted to have shown a picture to the witness which has the 65 ter number 4189. It's a photo showing Professor Seselj holding a gun and on his helmet is a White Eagle in front. If we can see this. Can we enlarge this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Witness, can you see what is on the helmet of Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the White Eagle insignia on the helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was this the typical insignia which also the volunteers had on their helmet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I've seen the White Eagle on a helmet. Usually they were caps. This is the first time I see a helmet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, Mr. Mussemeyer is deliberately trying to mislead the witness by equating the two-headed White Eagle as the traditional Serbian symbol or coat of arms with the paramilitary organisation called the White Eagles. The witness heard something about that organisation, but as he said he doesn't know any details. I think this is impermissible in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We took due note of what you have just said. According to you there could be a mix-up between the White Eagles who are a paramilitary unit and the White Eagle, which is -- which would be a symbol. You're saying that these are two different things. Witness, you've heard what was said. Can you add anything? If you have nothing to say, you just don't need to say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was just explaining about this photograph, that it was the first time I had seen the White Eagle on a helmet. I don't know of any direct connection between the White Eagles and the Serb Radical Party. I don't know whether there was any connection, and how strong it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small technical question. These White Eagles, the paramilitary unit which allegedly committed crimes, did you ever see any members of this unit in the street or encounter any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I couldn't tell them apart. In my view they were all the same. You couldn't tell by their uniforms or their insignia, because all these volunteers wore different insignia and different uniforms. It was all very varied, so it was very hard to say that they all belonged to a single group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but these volunteers in the broadest sense of the word, did you ever see any that had helmets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were volunteers with helmets which had five-pointed stars on them. Most helmets had that sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, you never saw a helmet with the White Eagle painted on it, except for the one we just saw on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour. It's the first time I've seen a helmet with a White Eagle on it. I've seen helmets with other insignia but not the White Eagle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: May I come back to the Exhibit number 936. There is one sentence on page 9 I want to have it commented by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I refer to paragraph 3 where it's said: "Chetnik members of a paramilitary group led by Vojislav Seselj were coming in small trucks packed with trunks of body bags." And then the sentence I will refer to is: "They spread rumours throughout the village that hundreds of Serbs have been massacred in Podravska Slatina and that they, the Serbs, will retaliate." Witness, are you aware of this fact and is it true? It's on page 10 of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw this report here, then I read this. As for rumours that in Slatina hundreds of Serbs had been massacred, all over Western Slavonia at the time, the part under Serb control, rumours were going around that in Daruvar, Pakrac, Grubisno Polje, Podravska Slatina, Pozega, Gradiska Nova, and other places, Serbs had been killed and taken away. So there were rumours about this happening. Later on it was established that a part of the Serbian population civilians did really end up that way. I heard about this only in the report and that revenge or retaliation would be carried out for the Serbs massacred in Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I think you should insist that the witness say what he thinks about this statement made allegedly by a witness, but there's no name mentioned here or not. Did any Seselj's men come there in small trucks loaded with body bags? Somebody stated this somewhere. It was included in the Helsinki Watch document. The Prosecutor is putting a question but we don't have the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Seselj. But this is a question that you should put during the cross-examination. It's up to you during cross-examination to highlight the inconsistencies. I see one immediately, and I will say it right away because I want it on the transcript. In the sentence in English it says: "Chetniks and (members of a paramilitary group led by Vojislav Seselj) were coming in small trucks," et cetera, et cetera. So very obviously the sentence that is in brackets has been put there by the person drafting the document. It's not the witness who said that. It's not Mr. Seselj that was with those trucks, you know, that had the body bags. So obviously something is added in brackets. Something has been added. But you can do this during the cross-examination. This is when you will have the opportunity to do this. I can't, you know, replace you at all moment and replace everyone. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I please have admitted the Exhibit number 4189 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P184.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: As for the video, it's my understanding that it has already been admitted, but we played a shorter version maybe that we need an additional exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P185.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, have there been destructions in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was burning of houses and blowing up of houses belonging to Croats or other non-Serbs during the war up to 1991. And then when the Serbs fled, the Croats burnt Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that in the report, that it had been destroyed. I've heard about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You never saw this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't there where the church was. Unfortunately, at the time it was the custom to destroy churches on a large scale, both Catholic and Orthodox. This was not an isolated incident. It was just one of many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to show the witness a map which has the 65 ter number 142. It's a map called "Crime Locations with Ethnic Composition."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Prosecutor, who drew this map? Could you source it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry, at the moment I have no answer to this but I will check it. According to our records, it's a document from the 17th of September, 2002, and it was admitted -- not admitted. It was brought into this institution by an investigator, as far as I can see. I think the name is not important of this investigator. This is all I can tell you about this, but I want to show this to the witness and let him tell us if, according to his information, this map is correct and what it does show.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
