utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, we don't know the source of the map. We only know that it was procured by an investigator of the OTP. Of course we're not interested in his name, but we have to know who drew up this map based on what data. How can the witness know whether the map is correct for each and every location? The witness can know that there were victims on both the Croat and the Serb side, and he can perhaps estimate in a general way where there were more victims, on which side, but as for the details on this map, the witness cannot do this. I couldn't do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Apparently it seems that it is the OTP who drew this map through an investigator. This must be the reason. I see that the source is on the bottom right. There's ERN numbers, and they must correspond to witness statements, victims' statements. So this is the reason. This document comes from the OTP and was drawn up using crimes committed in different localities as source. That's all we know. However, independently in all this, what is the purpose of your question, Mr. Prosecutor, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: For me Mr. Seselj's remarks are completely right, but I would like to hear this from, from the witness if he can show us or can tell us if this map, according to his information, is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute before answering, Witness. You may answer if you have knowledge. However, if you have no knowledge, just say so and say you cannot answer. I'm picking things at random. I see a settlement, Skabrnja, in the left, bottom left. It seems that there were Serb victims and a few Croats. So do you know something about this or do you know nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you mentioned the village of Skabrnja which is well known in Croatia, because a large-scale crime against Croatian civilians occurred there in 1991 in Vrbe [phoen]. About 40 people were killed in Skabrnja at the time and there was a trial where the perpetrators were prosecuted recently. As for the map, Your Honour, I can testify to the fact that I am familiar with the names of the villages mentioned here such as Saborsko, Vocin, Cetekovac, Balinci, and so on. I know them as places where crimes were committed against Croats. I'm referring to this map now. There were also other places where Serbs were victims. But in geographical terms, I think this map does indicate crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just said that in Skabrnja there was a trial. To your knowledge, was anyone convicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Several people were convicted, some in their absence. Others were brought to Croatia and tried there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these people who were found guilty, what unit did they belong to? Were they TO members? Did they belong to a paramilitary unit? Were they volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party? Who were these people who were convicted? The Prosecutor's showing us this -- this village, you know, and he's presenting his case. It's obviously because there was a connection with the accused. Otherwise, he just wouldn't show this. I'm trying to understand. Do you know who was convicted and do you know which unit these people convicted belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, Your Honour, it was said that they were members of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac municipality, I think. This crime was ascribed to the JNA and to the best of my knowledge the Territorial Defence of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question and I apologise for being so detailed but I feel obliged to do this. Crimes were committed by people who apparently were military. According to the knowledge you have of this event, was this done within a military context or were these crimes committed by individuals who might have been military but who committed the crimes on their own accord, individually without the JNA or the TO or this unit or that unit be implied? Could you shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards Skabrnja, there was the army there with its own commanders and there were also local people who were members of the Territorial Defence. I think that these crimes occurred because they were perpetrated by individuals who came from the local area, but what their motivation was, I don't know. I've heard different stories. If you listen to the Croatian side, they were simply venting their feelings on the population, whereas the Serbs say there was fighting and the civilians were killed in the fighting. I did not attend the trial, so I'm not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question. Witness, please, do you know whether the people who were convicted were convicted for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to draw attention to the fact that you may have lost from view the fact that a far greater crime was committed against Serbs in Skabrnja. The Serb victims were greater by three-quarters than the Croatian victims in numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that maybe so, but what we're interested in right now is to know whether on the -- this list of crimes is to know whether the perpetrators belonged to the JNA or to the TO. Apparently so. And what was the nature of the crimes committed, and it seemed that these were crimes of war. This is all we can draw from this at the moment, at the moment. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think this comes also out from this map, because if you see in Skabrnja there's three-quarter is red, which is for Serbs. So these were Serbs victims. I can give you additional information about this map. It has indeed been produced by the OTP, by OTP members, but based on statements from witnesses of this area. And from the 1991 census what -- that was the source of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Prosecutor, the problem with the pie chart, you know, hadn't escaped me. Of course I had wondered whether these pie charts dealt with the ethnic make-up of the casualties, and you just answered affirmatively, or whether these pie charts represented the ethnic make-up of the settlement itself and not of the casualties. But according to what you just said, in blue we have the Croat victims and in red the Serb victims. And there are a few towns, at least five, where there are other victims that are neither Croat nor Serbian. They're green.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Exactly. And if I may assist the Chamber, this map has been -- I know that it is of no importance for your Chamber, but this map has been admitted into evidence in the Milosevic case as Exhibit 326, tab 6. Can I have it admitted into evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We need a number and then we will record your objection. We have a number please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your objection, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this map being admitted because it is unprofessionally made. We have no indices to tell us what the circles represent which resemble the French cheese Camembert, as you say, or pie chart and what the figures are, and all the circles are the same so it would appear that an equal number of crimes were committed in all these locations. And then a selection is being made of the victims according to Serb victims, Croat victims and others, and it is impossible that the figures apply to all this, that they're the same. So this map is a falsification of its own, because these circles should be different in size, as far as I understand the technique of compiling graphics of this kind, whereas the circles are the same. So it's a hundred victims here, a hundred there and a hundred in the third place and that's the ratio, and that's impossible. So in fact this map tells us nothing. Now, if we're talking about the crime locations, then you can state the places. Without figures the map does not telling you anything. Letting -- leaving aside the fact that Mr. Mussemeyer is giving us the figures for all the casualties committed by the Serbs because I seem to be the culprit for all the victims and the JCE. Now, if I were -- if I had been the main commander of all the Serb forces, then that could be taken into consideration, but like this it can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are taking down your objection. Personally, I must say that these pie charts seem to connect different events for Skabrnja municipality, for example, where apparently there were Serb -- a great number of Serb victims, and the perpetrators were probably -- must have been Croats, and Croat victims who would have been killed by Serbs. But there must have been crimes that were committed in different periods of time. That's all we can say as it is now. But we now have the objection from Mr. Seselj on the transcript. Please continue, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to continue with the facts you already were asking for, if these crimes have ever been investigated and by whom, and for this purpose I want to show the witness the 65 -- the document under 65 ter 1026.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is a document by the military post of Banja Luka, security office, addressed to the military prosecutor, and it relates to the crimes committed in Vocin. Mr. Witness, do you know this document and can you tell us something about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the document here in the OTP when I came, and it does correspond to the events that took place, and I have heard that an investigation had been conducted into these events in the course of 1992. Witnesses were heard who were in the vicinity. Colonel and Lieutenant Colonel Stevilovic, he conducted the investigation into these events, I believe, but they weren't just events in Vocin. They were also in the village of Glavica, which is a village a little further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if something happened to the investigator Milan Stevilovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I heard sometime in 1992, I believe, he was killed in Republika Srpska, not far from Banja Luka, that he was killed by some extremist Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why he was killed or don't you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he conducted investigations all over the place. I think that it was when the war in Bosnia began and it was said that he poked his nose into things that shouldn't interest him. Otherwise, he was an honourable officer. Anyway, that's the story I heard linked to his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if ever trials were led against the alleged perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I have this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I have a question for the Prosecutor. An investigation was carried out by Lieutenant Colonel Stilovic [as interpreted] who seems to have been murdered in 1992. This report deals with a number of individuals and is sent to the military prosecutor in Banja Luka. Now, what happened to the investigation? Was there an investigative Judge? Were the perpetrators judged? Were they convicted? What happened afterwards, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really know what happened afterwards because he belonged to the Banja Luka Corps. Now, whether the military court in Banja Luka took any steps I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to avoid any misunderstanding, I'd like to draw your attention to the following: We're talking here about a group of people who are almost -- to a man from Novi Sad, which is symptomatic, asymptomatic indicator. Secondly, it says for each one of them that they were primarily volunteers, but they were at the military post 8316, 8316, which means that was the JNA, and according to that we can identify which JNA unit it was. And the Prosecutor is leading us astray and skipping that purposely. They were all from unit 8316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. This had not escaped me, and this is why I'm asking the question to the Prosecutor. What came out? Was there an outcome to the investigation? Do you know or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I can't tell you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an observation to make regarding Mr. Seselj when he takes floor. I'm saying this for himself, for his own interest. The risk is that we will not take what he is saying into account if he does not make his comment in the right moment during the cross-examination. It's like -- it's as if we were accepting that you testified, and we don't -- we will not allow this. So all these comments you're making will probably not be taken into account. You must try and obtain all this information, you know, that you aim at demonstrating during the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, what my fellow Judge is saying, and I already said this to you last week, if you're challenging something, if you're challenging the fact that these people were volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party, then it's very easy for you to do that. You have this report. You know -- you're aware of this report. You see that these people seem to belong to the -- to the unit 8316. Get the judgement, get all the documents and the files of the investigating judge and prove that these individuals either did this on their own accord or under orders of JNA and not because of a political -- because they were volunteers from a political party. But do this during the cross-examination. This is when you should lead all this, because as my fellow Judge is saying, we will note down your objection. We cannot draw any conclusions from it. The only conclusions we will draw from it is that we will compare this document with what you will demonstrate later on. This is exactly what I told you last week. Otherwise, what will happen is we have a document, if we don't have a counter document coming from you, we can draw the conclusion that "volunteers" committed crimes. And if we connect this document to other documents then we can end up by saying that these volunteers belonged to the Serbian Radical Party and this would all lead up to you. So during the cross-examination it will be your turn to challenge this evidence, but not just by comments but through documents that you will show. Technically this is very easy here in this case. Just check with the military prosecutor in Banja Luka, see what happened, what was the outcome of this case. Kulic, Milosevic, Kuga, Ristic, Stjepanovic -- find out what they said when they were on trial. I mean, those who are not on the loose, because obviously some are at large. I don't really know. But this is something you will do during the cross-examination. You can highlight the fact that all these people came from Novi Sad, had nothing to do with you, so forth and so on. Please proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to make a comment again. I oppose to having documents admitted and I explained why. Throughout the document nowhere does it say that these people were volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, and I can see that you've already drawn the conclusion that they were indeed volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. Secondly, here there is an abbreviation that is used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I have drawn no conclusion. I said that one could conclude something on the basis of the documents that would be cross-referenced. So you should be made aware of this, and you should deal with this during the presentation of your case when you rebut the Prosecution's case. This is what I wanted to tell you. And I put this in the conditional tense.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, Mr. President. You can see this abbreviation V/O at the end of the description of each of the accused. Now, this V/O wasn't interpreted, whereas V/O is an abbreviation used by the JNA which means military conscript. In the military post such-and-such number. So at one time he was a volunteer, then he was mobilised into the JNA and became a military conscript, V/O. And I'm not going to ask this witness anything during my cross-examination because this witness has nothing to do with the document. He's never seen the document before until he was shown it by the Prosecution. So I have a serious concept for my own cross-examination, and I'm not going to be led astray by these bits and pieces that the Prosecution is trying to infiltrate. It says military conscript for each of them, V/O, and that's not a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party. So I'm not going to put forward any counter-documents to prove the contrary. These are nebulous things. I have planned my defence seriously. I don't care who they are. Why should I show you who they are? I am not a prosecutor. I'm not going to take the role of subsequent prosecutor. All I'd like to do is to draw the Court's attention to the fact that you have no information that we're dealing here with members of the Serbian Radical Party. Now, if you admit this into evidence, fine. We can move on. I apologise for the comments I made, for my objection then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your observation is now on the record. Now, in light of what you have just said, I would like to tell you that in the report that was issued the commander of a unit of volunteers is mentioned. You are right in saying that these are military men, but there's a commander of a unit of volunteers that is mentioned in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The reason to show this document for me was that there have been investigations and that the leader of this investigations has been killed later on. I would like to have this document admitted into evidence and go on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Okay. The next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I would like to put the question of relevance then, because if you agree that the possible perpetrators of these crimes who were investigated according to this document were not members of the SRS or volunteers of the SRS, then what is the relevance of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It is the Prosecution's intention to show the whole picture, what really happened, to give a history, overview, and some documents not always relate to Mr. Seselj's volunteers, but it's necessary to give the Trial Chamber a complete overview about the events which happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has noted the Prosecution's comment and Mr. Seselj's objection. We'll mark the document for identification. Registrar, the 65 ter document 1026, could we have a document that is marked for identification. This document will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI P187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The next document I want to show to the witness is the 65 ter number 2078. It's a description of war crime events in accordance with the article of Criminal Code of the Croatian department of war crimes in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, can you please comment on this document? Is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it here and read it. Mention is made of the events in the area of Podravska Slatina, Vocin, and further afield. The name of Ilija Sasic is mentioned. The weapons are mentioned. The arming is mentioned. And the Prevenda hamlet of Vocin is mentioned, inhabited by the Croatian population. So that's what I actually heard about those events subsequently on the territory of Vocin as I said earlier on during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: At the bottom of this document it is said: "During the retreat of Chetniks." Can you tell us why the Serb forces retreated and the Serb inhabitants fled at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time there were frequent attacks by the Croatian police and army in the area. And as far as the TO of Daruvar is concerned, it withdraw earlier on because it wasn't able to defend itself from the frequent clashes between the Serb TO and the Croatian police and army in the Daruvar area, so that area was left open and it was insecure and unsafe. So when the territorials withdrew, the people also withdrew. The population withdrew because they were afraid that they would be killed. And there was an exodus there, too, from the area of Slatina, Orahovac, and Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know where these people were fleeing to, which areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in leaving Western Slavonia they would go via Banja Luka toward Serbia, Eastern Slavonia and Srem. Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I wanted to question if you have any information that some of them also fled to Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A part of the population ended up in Vojvodina. They went to various places in Vojvodina province, Subotica and then lower down, Sombor, Novi Sad, and so on. Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was also Hrtkovci mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer the Prosecutor's question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear it. I didn't hear the question. Could he repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You enumerated the regions where these witnesses were fleeing to and you also mentioned Vojvodina, enumerating certain villages. Did they flee also to Hrtkovci? Did you hear about it or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they went to Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the document we have before us is an interesting one. We would like you to give us some information about it. According to this document, in June 1990 [Realtime transcript read in error "1991"], in the municipality of Slatina there is an arm of the Serbian Democratic Party that is being established, and a lawyer, Ilija Sasic, heads it. It seems that after this was established some people in three localities, Sekulinci, Bucje, and Zvecevo, were trained. Also a fourth locality which was Ceralije. After that events occur and a terrorist unit which is qualified as such headed by Lukic and Radosavljevic will act. According to what you know -- in the transcript there is a mistake. I said June 1990, and I read 1991. You have to be very careful to the case. June 1990. That's what's written in the document. You who had specific knowledge about this, do you know whether the Serbian Democratic Party had established in Slatina an arm of the party where some members of this party trained, you can see what is written in the document, and what can you say about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS was founded in 1990, in June, on the territory of Podravska Slatina municipality. In the course of 1991, the Secretariat for National Defence, Slatina municipality, and the others that I enumerated, on their behalf mobilised the reservists, the military conscripts, and set up its headquarters in Vocin, Slatina, and so on, but they were in the area around Zvecevo and Vocin. Now, Lukic and Radosavljevic were the commanders of the TO Staffs, one for Slatina, one for Vocin as far as I recall, and they were in command of those TO units in that area. Now, how they armed them I don't know. Now, the party itself did not carry out arming. It was individuals who were organised within the frameworks of the secretariat of the -- of national defence that did so, and the name of Ilija Sasic is particularly mentioned, and they conducted military actions or operations in the area, stormed the villages which were mostly populated by the Croats. Now, the -- Sekulinci, Zvecevo, and so on are places that are mentioned. They grouped themselves militarily there, and when the TO units were formed attached to the staffs, they were deployed in the different localities to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what you are telling us, those people who headed those operations were members of the Serbian Democratic Party. That has nothing to do with the Radical -- Serbian Radical Party of Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Perhaps they weren't members of the Serbian Democratic Party. They had nothing to do specifically here with the Serbian Radical Party, and I think that they were organised in such a way -- let me repeat that the Secretariat of National Defence organised them for the Podravska Slatina municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get to the heart of the matter. According to you, the people in charge of this unit, Lukic and Radosavljevic, did they have any connection whatsoever with Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the time we're talking about, no. Whether they had contacts later on or anything to do with him later on I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to have admitted the last document which is number 2078 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that here in the English you don't have a list of the suspects. All it says is "List of suspects." Now, if you look at the Serbian list of suspects, it says there that there were 78 persons. All those 78 were locals of Western Slavonia, inhabitants of Western Slavonia. Not a single one was from Serbia. Not only were they not from the Serbian Radical Party and our volunteer but not from Serbia. So for the 78, the Croatian authorities give the particulars and they're all from Western Slavonia. Now, in the introductory document you have something that I consider to be very important. It keeps saying Chetniks, Chetniks, Chetniks. The Croats call all Serb forces Chetniks. As far as they were concerned, they were Chetniks for them even before the Serbian Radical Party volunteers arrived. The war began in mid-August there, and the volunteers arrived in mid-October. So for two months they were referring to them as the Chetniks. There was no mention of volunteers from the Serb Radical Party. Now, you see that what the Prosecution is using here. The document says that all the suspects were local inhabitants, whereas he is now wanting to tender this as proof and evidence against me and against the Serbian Radical Party. I don't know how much longer you're going to tolerate things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall have this document marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI P188.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: For the assistance of the Chamber, this document has been admitted in the Milosevic case under number 327, tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to continue with -- we spoke about Serbs fleeing from Western Slavonia in different directions to Serbia. My question, did Croats flee from Vojvodina to Croatia or to Western Slavonia? Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the war they did come in to Croatia from Vojvodina. Some arrived as volunteers and joined the Croatian army. Some said they were forced to leave and had to leave their places of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about exchange of houses between Croats from Serbia and Serbs from Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was that, too, an exchange of houses. Except that in Western Slavonia that could not be the case because the vast majority of Serb houses were destroyed in actual fact so that they exchanged properties with -- so that properties were exchanged in other places, not so much in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What can you tell us about the exchange of houses, how things happened, what kind of procedure was adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, mostly there were go-betweens. Sometimes people would contact each other directly, so the Serbs fleeing from Croatia to Serbia or Bosnia would try to exchange their property for Croats fleeing from Serbia or leaving Serbia and Bosnia and going to Croatia. That's what happened in the area around Zadar, Banja Luka, and parts of Croatia. Now, Western Slavonia itself while the war was still going on, it was impossible to exchange property there because the war engulfed the towns too. So this is something that took place later on. The exchanges took place subsequently where through the courts and the legal authorities they tried to legalise this. Now, what happened later on is that the Croats who exchanged their property with Serb property were able to legalise their property in Croatia and later on they realised their rights to have their property back that they'd left. Now, the Serbs that exchanged their property for the Croats were not able to legalise their property in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, because the law didn't allow them to do that because of the international community. So they lost their property in Croatia because the person they exchanged properties with had managed to register and get the title deeds to the property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just described to us an overview of how things happened. If I've understood you correctly, you said there were go-betweens or that the people amongst themselves came to a solution and found a way of exchanging their houses, the Serbians and Croatians. And you also added that there was even a legalisation of this. This was written in the law. Some Croats who had acquired property then asked the legal authorities to draft title deeds. So notwithstanding what you have just said, what I'm interested is this: When this exchange of houses happened, as far as you know, did people other than private individuals intervene in this process? For instance, any political party or the Serbian Radical Party would have played a role in this or had a hand in this? Did the government or the representatives of the government or local authorities, municipality, could they have had a hand in this to entice the Croatians to leave, to replace them by Serbs from Croatia? According to you, did the political or administrative authorities play any part in the exchange of property or flats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe not so directly or so publicly that you would be able to see, but I would say that when these people were fleeing from these places like Western Slavonia and arrived in some places like Hrtkovci, they, specifically Rade Cakmak [phoen] was mentioned, intimidated those people and they had to leave their houses. I couldn't see that directly, how the pressure was exerted on those people and who supported this intimidation and pressure, but I believe those people were not given enough protection to stay. Instead they succumbed to pressure, and it got worse when new waves of refugees came looking for accommodation. Who exactly directed the refugees to those Croat houses I really cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that the refugees that were arriving in great number could exert pressure on the owners of the houses or the flats so that they leave and so that they could take their place. Is that what you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. Somebody probably helped them at the local level. Whether they were individual people or members of a political party I don't know because I wasn't there, and I didn't have that kind of contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among the people you knew, can you give us an example of someone whom you knew who exchanged his or her house against somebody else's? Could you give us an example? You don't have to give us any names, but could you just give us an example, something that comes to mind straight away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a number of examples, although I cannot give you the exact name at this time because it's precisely to my organisation that people addressed themselves attempting to recover their property in the hinterland of Zadar, Sibenik, and other places from where people exchanged their property for property in Banja Luka. There are many of those names and I confuse them now, but there are perhaps exact records about people and cases. I can give you one name perhaps now but I'm afraid to get it wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. At the time, you were a member of a political party. According to what you've just said, I have a feeling that there were some people who came to you, this is what you just said, to ask for you to do something, to settle this kind of issue. Is that what you've just told me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I mentioned that, I meant later events from 1997 and 1998, to this day when the war stopped and people started returning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the years 1992, 1993, not after that. During the events my question relates to 1992, 1993. At that time, were people coming for assistance and addressing themselves to the political parties so that the exchange of houses and flats could take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. Nobody addressed me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know what the accused's approach to this exchange of houses was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did speak about that as one of the ways, but I cannot tell you anything specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When the conflict was over, had there been attempts that the refugees can turn back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a series of attempts and a series of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was your approach for this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time I worked for the return of refugees, even during the war. From 1993 to 1995 when there were no longer any conflicts and the United Nations were there, I worked for Serbs to return to Serb villages and Croats to return to Croat villages, for the police force to be made up of representatives of both peoples to protect all the people. And in 1993, 1994, 1995, I worked on that. And after -- after that period, I continued to work systematically for the return of refugees to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have there also been opponents to this return back of refugees, and who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the opponents of that policy were the political leaders in Knin primarily, Martic, Babic, and their entourage. The people in Benkovac, Gracac, Lapac, and Korenica who were in their inner circle. Otherwise, there was no support on other sides either. They mostly kept silent and didn't support my drive. The stand of the government was that what was held by Serbs militarily should be populated by Serbs and the same went for Croats. There was yet no official recognition of the policy that refugees should return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could we please see on the monitor Exhibit -- or 65 ter number 1680.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is a letter of Milan Martic written to the United Nations Protection Force and State Committee for Cooperation in which he threatens military actions if Croatians are allowed back in the areas of Skabrnja, Novi Grad, Prodragra [phoen]. Mr. Witness, do you know this letter from Mr. Martic? It is on page 2. Or, rather, page 3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this letter by Martic. I had seen it earlier. And that was generally the policy of Mr. Martic, that Croats -- Croat refugees should not return -- should not be allowed to return to their former places of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I have admitted this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, they are deceiving you as to the contents of the document. In this letter Mr. Martic is opposed to forced moving in by Croats to Skabrnja. I am underlining the word "forced." Forced settlement is not the only form of settlement. Of course if there is a political agreement, there should be implementation. And second, I would like to raise the question of relevance. What do I have to do with Skabrnja? The witness told you a moment ago that the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party were not present there at all, so what could this mean to my case, and what could I possibly cross-examine the witness on this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want to reply to this objection, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: In fact, it's said that: "We will be forced to prevent by force arrival of the territory of Republic of Serbian Krajina" but I understand forced arrival, that the Serb inhabitants are forced to accept the refugees. Is this the right interpretation or am I wrong, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will give a final number to this document signed by Mr. Martic and sent to UNPROFOR, because we have proof of the existence of this document. The relevance is that this has a connection with the movement of population.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P189.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will now come to the next issue. This is the Vance Plan. Mr. Witness, are you familiar with the Vance Plan, and what was the goal of this plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan was signed in Sarajevo between Croatia and Yugoslavia. The objective of that plan was to deploy peacekeeping forces in the war-affected areas, those three autonomous provinces. It was envisaged to disarm, to re-establish peace, to open up roads, to enable refugees to return, and to seek a political solution. That was it briefly. It was supposed to be implemented in the course of 1992. That is the beginning of the 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Seselj's approach to the Vance Plan was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he said that the Vance Plan was not the best solution offered to the Serbs because at that time Babic was a great opponent of the Vance Plan, and as far as I remember, his opinion was that for the time being there was no better solution so it should be accepted. So it was neither for or against, really. He said mainly that this should be accepted for lack of a better option.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter number 4123 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I have admitted this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P190.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have a last question before I would ask the Trial Chamber to go into --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Mr. President. Again this begs the question of relevance. The witness said that I was in favour of accepting the Vance Plan but not against, although I had objections to its contents. Why would this be relevant enough to be introduced into evidence? The plan is common knowledge. If I had opposed the plan, then it would make sense to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Don't just raise objections for the sake of raising objections. This document deals with the international conference on the former Yugoslavia. These are official documents. This is public -- in the public domain. It cannot be challenged. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: As I said, I have a last question, which is completely unrelated to the facts we were taking evidence before. Mr. Witness, you mentioned in your first statement from May 2002, a person called Branko Popovic that was on the Regional Board of the SDS of Slavonia. Do you happen to know if this Branko Popovic later went to Zvornik and became the head of the TO there in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Branko Popovic, who led the SDS of Grubisno Polje was not pushing for war. He was a quiet, nice man who was in favour of a peaceful solution, and he was not a leader of any military formations. Later he died after the war, but he was a quiet, peaceful man, as I said, and he never led any military units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I believe that an objection in principle is in order. The question was too leading. Of course the witness answered with sobriety and calm, but you can't ask questions like this. Do you know that Branko Popovic went to Zvornik and put himself at the head of some military formations? This should not be done in an adversarial proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this question is slightly leading. You should have asked the witness whether to his knowledge Mr. Popovic went to certain places, and he would have said yes, and you could have said what places and so on and so forth. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I am done now with all the facts in open session. I would like to turn back into private session because I have some questions to the witness which might reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We are in open session. The Prosecutor has just informed us that he's completed his examination-in-chief. I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Seselj for him to start his cross-examination, and the Chamber had granted him four hours to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. VS-004, you spoke about the arrival of volunteers of the Serb Radical Party to Western Slavonia, and you spoke about my visit to Western Slavonia. How many times have you and I met?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think maybe on two occasions officially.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Seselj's microphone be switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that we met on two occasions officially. When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, I think, in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have to keep switching on. I don't know what's wrong with the microphone. In 1991 to the best of my recollection, we met on two occasions, once at a rally in Banja Luka in the Borik hall where there were several thousand people, and on the second occasion in Western Slavonia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have to keep switching it on. You attended that rally in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And where did we meet in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 we met, I think, in the Assembly of Yugoslavia when that convention was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was the convention on the third Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did we talk on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We only saw one another. Our only conversation was when I visited Western Slavonia at the dinner prepared for me by the leadership there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you recall what we spoke about at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, general issues, nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was Colonel Trbojevic, the commander of the Territorial Defence, present at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Colonel Trbojevic praise the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, saying they were very brave and disciplined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there any discussion of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did any of the officials of Western Slavonia at the time, and the entire leadership was there, the prime minister, the speaker of the Assembly, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, all the main officials were there; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did any of them have any complaints about the behaviour and discipline and conduct of the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not mentioned at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear me while I was in Western Slavonia advocate the commission of crimes, any sort of crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall you saying any such thing in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that I advocated the killing of civilians, the killing of prisoners of war, the expulsion of civilians, rapes, looting, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one ever told me that about you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about most of my political speeches in the wartime period where I categorically opposed any form of crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the war I did not have occasion to hear most of your speeches. I only heard some of them, but I never heard you call people to kill.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, a new form of gymnastics has been introduced here. Every time I start to speak I have to press this button. This has not been the practice so far. So far it's only been sufficient for me to press it once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, when I want to speak I also have to switch on my microphone. We're all supposed to do that when we want to take the floor. But I'm being told that since the witness has been granted voice distortion, we have to do this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand that now, and I'll act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the course of the examination-in-chief you mentioned that the territory of Western Slavonia was mostly a partisan area in World War II; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were no Chetniks there at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The vast majority of the Croats there were in the Ustasha, many of them were in the Home Guard, and as the war went on more and more Croats joined the partisans; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1941 there were very few Croats in the partisans, few pre-war Communists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1943 after the capitulation of Italy, when it was already well known that Hitler was going to lose the war, more and more Croats joined the partisans; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Members of the Ustasha units almost never joined the partisans; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was the Home Guard who joined the partisans. They were people who had been forcibly mobilised into units of the Independent State of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just before the end of the war, the Ustasha authorities mobilised a certain number of Serbs into the Home Guard by force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they did not give weapons to those Serbs. They were labour units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After World War II under the Communist regime, people from Western Slavonia were able to hear only negative things about Chetniks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Never anything positive. That's why there was fear of the Chetniks, fear of Serbs, Chetniks a priori; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's why the Serbs from Western Slavonia had mixed feelings when receiving volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they felt very threatened, which is why the volunteers were welcomed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were being threatened by the regime of Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, now we'll deal with the period right after the arrival of Franjo Tudjman and the Croatian Democratic Union in power. I will put brief questions to you, and please continue answering briefly and then we'll save a lot of time. As soon as Tudjman gained power, intensive renewal of Ustasha iconography started at political rallies and in public places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But before Tudjman's gaining power at the election rallies of his party, Ustasha symbols were brought out more and more often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that long before the war, long before gaining power, Franjo Tudjman entered into firm contacts with the Croatian Ustasha emigres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was Franjo Tudjman financed by the Ustasha emigres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he bring a leader of the Ustasha emigres to Croatia and make him minister of defence when he gained power?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that Gojko Susak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had he been a Ustasha leader among the emigres for a long time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long he had been a leader but he was an emigre leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you read Tudjman's book, "Worldlessness [phoen] of History"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard that Tudjman stated in public that he was proud that his wife was neither a Serb nor a Jew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So Franjo Tudjman displayed animosity both towards Serbs and towards Jews; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how people experienced it, how they perceived it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that Franjo Tudjman spoke in public that the Ustasha Independent State of Croatia, in the course of World War II, was also an expression of the historical aspiration of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the eyes of the public was this perceived as rehabilitation of the Ustasha state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did this inspire horror among the Serbian masses in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did this influence their fear or was it because I was scaring them with Tudjman from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were certainly afraid of these statements made by Mr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the mass of the Serbian people, did the new Tudjman regime represent a certain kind of restoration of the Independent State of Croatia? Is that how most Serbs perceived it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And at the parliamentary elections in Croatia, who did the Serbs vote for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave the greatest support to the -- to the League of Communists party, the Party of Democratic Changes of Ivica Racan, and only five representatives of the Serb Democratic Party entered parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that the majority of Serbs did not vote for their national party? They voted instead for the then ruling political party which was made up mostly of Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that Serbs primarily wanted stability, a peaceful and normal life together with Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that among the Serbian masses there was no great nationalist sentiment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Serbs feel betrayed by Racan's Party of Democratic Changes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they disenchanted by their behaviour before and after the elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were disappointed after the elections by his behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it only then that the Serbs joined the Serb Democratic Party en masse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's after May 1990. You made a mistake in the examination-in-chief. You said Tudjman's party came into power in end 1989, but Tudjman actually came into power in end April and early May 1990. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know it was an honest mistake, and I didn't want to draw attention to it. That year, 1990, when Tudjman came into power did you Serbs in the territory of Croatia even know about me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was I able to exert any influence to enhance your nationalist moods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990, was the name of Seselj familiar to those Serbs who lived in Croatia? Did that name ring a bell, or was it someone no one knew nothing about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was completely unknown to Serbs in Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that year 1990, after the electoral victory in Croatia, Tudjman speedily changes the situation in that republic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, he changed the official symbols of Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He abolished the red five-pointed stars, and the Serbs did not mind much because we've all -- we had already been sick and tired of it under Communist power.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not mind because they were loyal to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Especially in that partisan area where you lived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That five-pointed star was a symbol of struggle against Fascism and Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were not much interested in Communist ideology, but they were anti-fascists and they wanted to live in a normal state, and they wanted to be equal to Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Serbs in Croatia after World War II represent a constituent people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was the percentage of Serbs in Croatia approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirteen per cent, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just after World War II was there many more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a lot more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And before World War II there were even -- even more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time there were 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So from 30 per cent they fell to 12, 13 per cent. What explains that demographic fall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Ustasha crimes during the war, and then a number of people left Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After World War II?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did those people leave after World War II?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of them left to find jobs elsewhere, better living conditions, because their localities were underdeveloped and there were no great prospects.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did the authorities keep them underdeveloped deliberately in many of these regions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how we Serbs perceived it, that our regions were kept underdeveloped and neglected by the authorities in Croatia although Serbs were represented in those authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did it mean to have the status of a constituent nation, a constituent people? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that we were not a national minority as we were supposed to be after Tudjman came in power. We were an equal people, equal to Croats, enjoying all the rights guaranteed by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was the first time, do you know, when Serbs were proclaimed to be a people, a nation on equal footing in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're an educated man. Let me try to remind you. Was it in the 19th century?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it the basic precondition for the unification of the military Krajina with Croatia and Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The military Krajina, was this an independent territory under the direct government of Vienna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that military Krajina, Serbs border guards lived for centuries. They had no feudal obligations, but they served as good fighters against the Turks; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Under Austria and Hungary, Croatia was reduced to three counties only, Zagreb, Krizevac, and Varazdin; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After that Croats displayed political aspirations to unite with Slavonia; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there came the turn of military Krajina that encompassed current Dalmatia, Lika, Banija, Kordun, and Western Slavonia; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And to join Croatia and Slavonia, the Serbs put -- imposed a condition that they should be an equal people and as such represented in the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That first session of the anti-fascist council of the national liberation of Croatia, did it introduce the constituent status of Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did it mean that the legal status of Croatia may not be changed without the agreement and consent of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did this anti-fascist council of the national liberation of Croatia try also in this way to make reparations to Serbs because of the genocide committed against them in World War II?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Being a constituent nation, it was defined in the constitution that the State of Croatia belongs to Croat people and the Serbs who live in Croatia, just as all other people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did that imply that Croatia can never secede from Yugoslavia without the consent of the Serbs living in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Franjo Tudjman, as soon as he came into power, call into question the Serbs' status as constituent nation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To that end did he seek constitutional amendments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could Serbs ever agree to Tudjman's intentions to reduce them from a constituent nation to a simple national minority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs did not want to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your opinion, is that the basic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj is now dealing with a constitutional issue. He asked you a question, you answered yes but without making any further comment. His theory is as follows considering those questions: In the constitution mention was made of the Serb people, and the simple fact that Croatia would secede from Yugoslavia would have required the approval of a Constitution or a Serb constitutional Assembly. When Croatia decided to secede from Yugoslavia, were there internal discussions in Croatia, discussions related to the fact that Serbs had not been asked for their opinions? Did politicians mention the fact? Was there mention of this in the press? Were there demonstrations? To your knowledge did such things happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when the constitutional amendments initiated by Franjo Tudjman occurred requiring Serbs to be proclaimed a national minority rather than a constituent people, we from the Serbian Democratic Party proposed our own amendments to the constitution, invoking this anti-fascist council session insisting that we should stay a constituent nation precisely because of the role that Serbs played in the Croatian history even before the Second World War and especially during the Second World War when they were greatly victimised and they were the main anti-fascist force. However, the parliament did not acknowledge our proposals and the ruling party, Tudjman's party, Croatian democratic -- the HDZ, had a majority, and they pushed whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mention amendments to the Constitution. Was there a vote at the Assembly, at the parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our amendments were not even taken into consideration. If a proposal is not accepted, then there is no vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The amendments were dismissed as part of what kind of procedure, in a small circle, as part of a more official setting? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The proposals were not accepted or taken into consideration. Anything that came from the Serbian Democratic Party was rejected with -- dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In view of the way Croatia was founded after World War II, was it possible to change the status of Serbs within Croatia by simple out-voting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So in order to change the status of the Serbian people Serbian consent was required; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After the HDZ party came into power, they immediately started introducing new systemic laws.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they discriminatory regarding Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some laws like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was, for instance, the law on holidays where Serbs and Jews did not have the same right to celebrate their religious holidays.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not only Serbs but Jews as well, because they were required, first of all, to become members of a particular community in order to exercise the right to a holiday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In addition to those laws, the government of the Croatian Democratic Union also passed decrees which changed the current situation regarding inter-ethnic relations even quicker.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They introduced the coat of arm -- or coats of arms that were very reminiscent to Serbs of the Independent State of Croatia, the Ustasha state.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs perceived it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you -- do you remember the change of name of the academy of fine arts and science? It was renamed into Croatian academy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that this academy was called the Yugoslav academy of arts and science, and it was founded by Strossmayer and Racki in 19th century.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Only the Ustasha leader Pavelic tried to change the name of that academy before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it the case that in the new Statute of the Croatian academy of arts and science it was written that it was a successor of the academy from the times of Ustasha power, Ustasha government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Ustasha -- sorry. Did new Croatian authorities start renaming very quickly places, streets, squares, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the new names evoke former Ustasha criminals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there a big scandal with the raising of a monument to the Ustasha leader Mile Budak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Croatian media did open propaganda of separatism begin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did new Croatian authorities begin massive dismissals of Serbs from public service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Serbs lose their jobs in the police, in the judiciary, the television en masse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Many Serbs were forced to retire early, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Serbs began to be dismissed from large enterprises.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it the case that Tudjman's authorities introduced a new special document that had never existed before, and it was called Domovnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was for citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they issue it selectively to the citizens of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning it was hard for Serbs to get that document, that certificate of citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was hard even for Serbs whose fathers and grandfathers were born in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Serbs perceive the introduction of this certificate of citizenship, Domovnica as a way to expel them from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 21st of February, 1991, did the Croatian parliament adopt the decision that Federal laws no longer apply in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it by that time an openly separatist move?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how Serbs perceived it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just after he came into power, did Tudjman begin to arm the followers of his party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did it arrive in trailers massively from Hungary this weaponry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we could read in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you watch on television sometime in January 1991, a programme filmed by the counter-intelligence service of the JNA led by General Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was broadcast on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did this programme document the illegal arming of Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who General Martin Spegelj was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he was minister of defence in Tudjman's government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The military security service clandestinely taped some conversations between Martin Spegelj and his associates.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-004 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.
